overview: I2102 turns the basic scan from I2101 into emergency and approach-pattern work. The event standard is to keep the aircraft under control in IMC, then use disciplined power, attitude, trim, timing, and configuration changes through the GCA and S-1 patterns.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: IMC emergency discussion starts with control and judgment, not checklist recitation. Stabilize the aircraft, build the instrument scan, then solve the emergency.

children.text: NATOPS emergency procedures are the best available procedures, but they do not replace pilot judgment when weather, terrain, multiple malfunctions, or crew status change the problem.
The basic emergency order is maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation, take proper action, and land as soon as conditions permit.
Critical action or memory items come first when required; time permitting, back them up with the checklist to ensure completeness.
Brief how the answer changes between VMC and IMC. In IMC, altitude, terrain clearance, ATC coordination, and spatial-disorientation risk usually matter before local troubleshooting convenience.

For inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or an IMC abort, maintain aircraft control, transition fully to instruments, and climb immediately toward the applicable ERAA or local safe-altitude guidance as conditions permit; squawk as required and tell ATC your intentions.
Do not rush into switches or a full emergency procedure while the aircraft is still not stabilized on instruments.
The pilot at the controls maintains aircraft control and executes critical action memory items and any actions directed by the PIC.
Use CRM early: verbalize the aircraft state, the altitude plan, the emergency, and what help you need from ATC or the other cockpit.
A good brief explains the first safe altitude, the transponder or radio call, and what would make the event a land-as-soon-as-practical or more urgent problem.

items.text: The GCA pattern packages radar-approach skills into one airwork profile: downwind, turns, BAC transition, controlled descent, heading corrections, missed approach, and level-off.

children.text: Start at 200 KIAS, clean, on a cardinal heading and base altitude to simulate radar downwind.
Turn standard rate, not to exceed 30 degrees AOB, for 90 degrees of heading change; maintain altitude and use the one-third rollout rule.
Slow toward 150 KIAS with about 15% torque, anticipate left rudder, trim through the deceleration, and stabilize near 33% torque at 150 KIAS.
Make the second same-direction 90-degree standard-rate turn, again preserving altitude and leading rollout with the one-third rule.
Maintain heading and altitude while transitioning to BAC: reduce power to about 15%, check below 150 KIAS, lower gear and set flaps to T/O.
Expect added lift with flaps; use slight nose-low pressure to hold altitude and trim right rudder plus up elevator as the aircraft slows.
Execute the Before Landing Checklist and stabilize at 120 KIAS with about 42% torque.
After stabilizing, set about 24% torque, let the nose fall enough to hold 120 KIAS, and establish roughly 600 FPM for a 2000-foot simulated GCA descent.
The instructor may give 3- to 10-degree heading changes during the descent; do not let the corrections disrupt airspeed or rate.
Remember the FTI control split: nose controls airspeed and power controls rate of descent, but each input affects the other.
After the 2000-foot descent, execute the missed approach: max power, right rudder, and 10 to 15 degrees nose high.
Check VSI and altimeter for positive climb, call two positive rates and raise the gear.
Above 110 KIAS, raise the flaps; report gear and flaps up before 150 KIAS, then set 8 to 10 degrees nose high and accelerate toward 180 KIAS.
Climb for 2000 feet on the last assigned heading, then start the 200 KIAS cruise transition about 200 feet before level-off.
The maneuver is complete at the original altitude, 200 KIAS, and the last assigned heading.
Common errors are poor power/nose coordination in the descent, over-rotating on the missed approach, late gear or flap cleanup, and weak rudder trim that lets heading drift.

items.text: The S-1 pattern is a timing and scan drill: hold 150 KIAS and heading while flying two 1000-foot descents and two 1000-foot climbs at about 1000 FPM.

children.text: Start clean at 150 KIAS on any numbered or cardinal heading.
Use timing checkpoints every 250 feet; at 1000 FPM each 250-foot altitude change should take about 15 seconds.
Lead the clock by 3 seconds before 00 or 30 seconds so the new power and attitude picture is established on time.
For the descent, reduce power to about 15%, lower the nose to about 0 degrees, anticipate left rudder, and re-trim.
Maintain 150 KIAS with nose attitude and adjust power as required for rate.
At each 250 feet, check the clock for 15 seconds elapsed and decide whether you are ahead or behind.
Three seconds before the end of one minute or 50 feet before the end of the 1000-foot descent, whichever occurs first, add power to about 55% and raise the nose to about 6 degrees nose high.
Anticipate right rudder, re-trim, then continue to hold 150 KIAS with pitch and use power to correct the climb rate.
At the next transition, repeat the descent and climb using the same 3-second lead and 50-foot level-off cue.
About 50 feet before the final altitude, transition to level flight at 150 KIAS on the original altitude regardless of rate.
The maneuver is complete when heading, altitude, airspeed, and trim are stable after the second climb.
Pitch primarily controls airspeed and power primarily controls vertical rate, but changing one will still affect the other.
Common errors are weak rudder trim, late or incorrect power settings, swapping pitch and power roles, and confusing ahead versus behind timing corrections.

studyNotes.summary: Prioritize aircraft control and safe-altitude decision making first, then fly the GCA and S-1 patterns with disciplined power, attitude, trim, timing, and configuration calls.

summary: IMC emergency priorities, GCA pattern execution, and S-1 timing discipline.
